coverage_conditions.text: Applies to residential rental dwellings and units statewide, including mobilehome park units, unless an exemption applies. Housing with a certificate of occupancy issued within the previous 15 years is exempt. Housing under a stricter local rent control is exempt. Owner-occupied two-unit properties and separately alienable properties with qualifying non-corporate owners are exempt.

rules.effective_date_text: This section shall become operative on April 1, 2024.
exemptions: Housing restricted as affordable housing by deed, regulatory agreement or other recorded document, or covered by a housing subsidy agreement for very low, low or moderate income households
Dormitories owned and operated by an institution of higher education or a K-12 school
Housing subject to a public entity's rent or price control that limits annual increases to less than the state cap
Housing issued a certificate of occupancy within the previous 15 years, unless it is a mobilehome

rules.key_value: Annual increase capped at the lower of 5% plus local CPI change or 10%; at most two increases per 12 months; operative 2024-04-01; repealed 2030-01-01
rules.quoted_span: an owner of residential real property shall not, over the course of any 12-month period, increase the gross rental rate for a dwelling or a unit more than 5 percent plus the percentage change in the cost of living, or 10 percent, whichever is lower
rules.requirement: An owner of residential real property may not raise the gross rental rate for a dwelling or unit by more than 5 percent plus the local percentage change in the cost of living, or 10 percent, whichever is lower, over any 12-month period. The base is the lowest gross rental rate charged in the 12 months before the increase takes effect. A tenant who stays in occupancy may not be given more than two increases in a 12-month period. The owner may set the initial rent for a new tenancy, and the cap applies to later increases. Owners must give notice of increases under Section 827. Waivers of these rights are void. Tenants may recover injunctive relief, damages and attorney's fees, and up to three times the overcharge for willful violations. The section is operative April 1, 2024 and is repealed on January 1, 2030.

coverage_conditions.text: Applies statewide to rental property owners, coordinators and other persons dealing with residential dwelling units in New Jersey, which include houses, apartments, accessory units and other primary-residence units.

rules.effective_date_text: This act shall take effect on the first day of the twelfth month next following the date of enactment.
exemptions: Spreadsheets that operate without artificial intelligence and require human analysis are not algorithmic devices
Databases that only use an algorithm to query unprocessed data are not algorithmic devices
Coordinating function excludes research, statistical analysis or testing that is not used to set or recommend rents or lease terms
Coordinating function excludes publicly available rent estimates provided at no cost
Coordinating function excludes real estate brokerage databases available on equal terms that do not set or recommend rents or collect competitively sensitive information to do so
Government entities setting or limiting rents through affordability controls are excluded from coordinator and coordinating function
Residential dwelling unit excludes inpatient medical care, licensed long-term care, and detention or correctional facilities
rules.key_value: Unlawful to use or operate algorithmic rent-setting coordinators (violation of the NJ Antitrust Act)
rules.quoted_span: any person to perform a coordinating function
rules.requirement: It is unlawful, and a violation of the New Jersey Antitrust Act, for a rental property owner (or its agent or subcontractor) to pay for or subscribe to a coordinator's services. It is also unlawful for a coordinator to facilitate an agreement among rental property owners that restricts competition, for two or more persons to engage in or facilitate parallel pricing coordination, and for any person to perform a coordinating function. A coordinator is a person who operates algorithmic revenue management software or an algorithmic device that sets or recommends rental prices, material lease terms or occupancy levels using the competitively sensitive information of other owners. The Attorney General receives complaints and may adopt rules. Municipalities may not enact ordinances that conflict with the act.
rules.title: Forbidding the Algorithmic Inflation of Rent (FAIR) Act
